Chapter 3: The Influence of Culture on Personal Values.
Every generation gets shaped by the world it grows up in. The values we hold, the goals we chase, and even how we see ourselves—these are all touched by the culture that surrounds us.
Lately, there’s been a real shift, hasn’t there? It seems like everywhere you look, the spotlight is on individualism and self-promotion. From the time we’re kids, we hear things like, “Find your passion,” “Stand out from the crowd,” or “Make a name for yourself.” Ambition’s not a bad thing—far from it—but when we focus so much on ourselves, it can push aside the deeper work of building real character.
Picture a teenager scrolling through social media, seeing endless images of success and perfection. The message is loud and clear: if you want to matter, you’ve got to be seen, admired, maybe even envied. It’s so easy to start measuring your worth by the number of followers, likes, or awards you collect.
But chasing that kind of validation? It can leave you feeling anxious, insecure, and weirdly disconnected from your own true values.
And it’s not just online. This culture of self-promotion sneaks into schools, workplaces, even our conversations about what it means to be successful. There’s this subtle pressure to always look like you’ve got it together—to show off your best self, and hide any hint that you might be struggling.
Over time, that gets exhausting. It makes it tough to be honest about what’s really going on, or to admit you need help, or even to say, “Hey, I’m having a hard time.”
And yet, under the surface, most people want something deeper. We all want to feel connected, to belong, and to live lives that truly matter. The tricky part? Our culture doesn’t always make room for those kinds of goals. It’s so much easier to chase after likes and applause than to do that slow, sometimes uncomfortable work of figuring out who we really are.
I’ll share a story with you. There was a college student who spent years chasing top grades and leadership roles, thinking that’s what mattered most. But one day, she realized she didn’t even know what she truly valued anymore. Her resume looked amazing, but she’d lost sight of her own interests and passions. So, she took a break. She started volunteering, spent time reflecting, and talked with people from all sorts of backgrounds. That’s when she began to rediscover what really mattered to her. It wasn’t always easy—in fact, it was pretty unsettling—but it set her on a path toward living out her own values, instead of just meeting everyone else’s expectations.
Most of us end up facing a moment like that. The world keeps telling us to chase success, but deep down, we’re searching for meaning. Balancing those two? It’s not always simple. You might get caught up in the race for achievement, only to realize later that something important got left behind.
Culture has a powerful pull, but it’s not the whole story. We have the ability to choose which values to hold onto, and which ones we want to question. That’s not always a straight line. It takes courage, honesty, and a willingness to go against the flow sometimes. But if you set aside a little time to reflect, to really listen to your own inner voice—and seek out people who live out the virtues you admire—you can build a life that’s not just successful, but deeply meaningful too.
In the end, the journey toward character is a bit like swimming upstream. It’s about resisting the urge to always be “on,” to always reach for more—and instead, focusing on the quieter, steadier work of becoming a better person. You don’t have to give up ambition. Just put it in its right place: serve others, build community, and live with real integrity.
